name: DEPDC5 familial focal epilepsy with variable foci
aliases: familial focal epilepsy with variable foci

clinicalPearls: Caused by usually heterozygous loss-of-function variants in DEPDC5, a component of the GATOR1 complex that acts as a negative regulator of the mTOR signalling pathway
Produces autosomal dominant familial focal epilepsy with variable foci, in which affected relatives have focal seizures arising from different cortical regions
Penetrance is incomplete, so some variant carriers are seizure-free, which complicates family counselling and interpretation of pedigrees
Seizures are focal and include frontal, temporal, and other lobar semiologies, often nocturnal, and may be sleep-related hypermotor in type
A subset of patients have focal cortical dysplasia or other malformations of cortical development, sometimes as a somatic second-hit lesion amenable to epilepsy surgery
There is a notably increased risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, which should be discussed with families and factored into management
Because DEPDC5 disinhibits mTOR, mTOR inhibitors are of mechanistic and investigational interest for refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: DEPDC5 is part of the GATOR1 complex, which inhibits mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) signalling, a pathway controlling cell growth, protein synthesis, and neuronal excitability. Loss-of-function variants relieve this inhibition, causing constitutive mTOR pathway overactivity. In the brain this promotes epileptogenesis and, when a somatic second hit occurs in a clone of cells, can produce focal cortical dysplasia. The dominant germline variant with incomplete penetrance explains the familial focal epilepsy with variable foci, while mTOR overactivation underlies both the seizures and associated cortical malformations and provides a rationale for mTOR-directed therapy.

additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the DEPDC5 variant, with segregation across the family
High-resolution epilepsy-protocol brain magnetic resonance imaging to detect focal cortical dysplasia
Prolonged video electroencephalography to localise variable seizure foci
Presurgical evaluation where a resectable dysplastic lesion is identified
Consideration of somatic mosaicism testing of resected tissue
Family history documentation and genetic counselling for incomplete penetrance
redFlags: Drug-resistant focal seizures with a potentially resectable cortical lesion
Features suggesting elevated sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
Frequent nocturnal seizures with injury or respiratory risk
reference.prognosis: Many carriers have well-controlled or even subclinical disease due to incomplete penetrance, but a subset have drug-resistant focal epilepsy; surgical resection of an identified dysplastic focus can be curative, and the recognised sudden unexpected death risk affects overall outcome.
pitfalls: Interpreting a seizure-free carrier as unaffected and misjudging recurrence risk given incomplete penetrance
Missing subtle focal cortical dysplasia on standard imaging
Failing to counsel about the heightened sudden unexpected death in epilepsy risk
Overlooking surgical candidacy in drug-resistant focal disease
references: ILAE resources on GATOR1/mTOR-related focal epilepsies
management: Control focal seizures with standard focal-onset antiseizure medication such as carbamazepine, lamotrigine or levetiracetam
Pursue presurgical evaluation and resective epilepsy surgery when drug-resistant seizures arise from a defined focal cortical dysplasia
Consider mTOR-directed therapy with agents such as everolimus, given the constitutive mTOR pathway overactivity that underlies the disorder
Counsel on the recognised risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy and provide seizure-safety advice
Coordinate epileptology, neurosurgery and neuroradiology with high-resolution epilepsy-protocol MRI and video electroencephalography
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and undertake family segregation testing
